items.followUp: Distinguish between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout.
rubric.description: States that a homogeneous mixture has uniform composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing its composition as uniform or the same throughout.

rubric.why: A heterogeneous mixture does not have uniform composition throughout.
rubric.description: States that a heterogeneous mixture has non-uniform composition or distinguishable parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing its composition as non-uniform or its components as distinguishable.

modelAnswer: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout.
A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition, and its different parts may be distinguished.

items.followUp: Define isotopes and give the isotopes of hydrogen.

rubric.why: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
rubric.description: Defines isotopes in terms of atomic and mass numbers, or protons and neutrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both what is the same and what is different.

rubric.why: The two common isotopes of chlorine have mass numbers 35 and 37.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving both chlorine isotopes.

modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
The isotopes of chlorine are chlorine-35 (³⁵Cl) and chlorine-37 (³⁷Cl).

items.followUp: Describe Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom.

rubric.why: The model described the atom as a sphere of positive charge.
rubric.description: States that the atom is a sphere or mass of positive charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the positively charged sphere idea.

rubric.why: Electrons were thought to be embedded in the positive sphere, making the atom neutral overall.
rubric.description: States that electrons are embedded or distributed within the positive charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing the electrons' arrangement in the positive sphere.

modelAnswer: According to the plum pudding theory, an atom is a sphere of positive charge.
Electrons are embedded in this sphere, making the atom electrically neutral overall.

items.followUp: Why are noble gases generally chemically stable?

rubric.why: Noble gases have complete outermost electron shells.
rubric.description: Identifies the complete outermost electron shell of noble gases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that their valence shell is complete.

accept: do not gain or lose electrons
rubric.why: With a stable electron arrangement, they have little tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons.
rubric.description: Connects the complete shell to their low reactivity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that they have little or no tendency to react by transferring or sharing electrons.

modelAnswer: Noble gases have complete outermost electron shells (helium has a complete duplet; the others have an octet).
This stable arrangement means they have little tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons, so they are not reactive.

items.followUp: Explain how shielding affects the removal of an outer-shell electron.

rubric.why: Inner-shell electrons shield outer electrons from the full positive charge of the nucleus.
rubric.description: Explains that inner electrons shield valence electrons from nuclear attraction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking inner electrons or the shielding effect to reduced nuclear attraction on outer electrons.

rubric.why: The reduced attraction makes an outer electron easier to remove, allowing a cation to form.
rubric.description: Connects shielding to easy electron removal or cation formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that shielding makes electron removal and cation formation easier.

modelAnswer: Inner-shell electrons shield the outermost electrons from the full attraction of the nucleus.
The outer electrons are therefore less strongly held and can be removed easily to form a cation.

items.followUp: State and explain the trend in ionization energy down a group.

rubric.why: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.description: Gives the direction of the ionization-energy trend across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it increases across the period from left to right.

rubric.why: Increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic radius strengthen attraction to the outer electron.
rubric.description: Gives a reason for the increase across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the trend to increasing nuclear attraction, increasing nuclear charge, or decreasing atomic radius.

modelAnswer: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
This is because nuclear charge increases and atomic radius generally decreases, so the outer electron is attracted more strongly to the nucleus.

items.followUp: What is metallic bonding? Explain why metals conduct electricity.

rubric.why: Metal valence electrons are delocalized and are not confined to individual atoms.
rubric.description: Identifies the freely moving or delocalized valence electrons in metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that valence electrons are free, mobile, or delocalized.

rubric.why: Mobile electrons carry charge through the metal when an electric field is applied.
rubric.description: Connects the mobile electrons to electrical conduction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that these electrons move through the metal and carry charge.

modelAnswer: The valence electrons in metals are delocalized and can move freely among the positive metal ions.
When an electric field is applied, these mobile electrons move through the metal and carry electric charge.

items.followUp: What is a polar covalent bond, and how does it form?

rubric.why: A difference in electronegativity causes the shared electrons to be attracted unequally.
rubric.description: Explains that unequal sharing of electrons results from a difference in electronegativity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking unequal electron sharing to different electronegativities.

rubric.why: Unequal sharing produces partial charges at opposite ends of the molecule, forming a dipole.
rubric.description: States that opposite partial charges or poles develop.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the positive and negative ends or partial charges.

modelAnswer: A dipole develops when atoms in a molecule have different electronegativities and share electrons unequally.
This creates a partial positive end and a partial negative end in the molecule.
